\section[graduarse]{graduarse — to graduate}

\label{lesson:ES-C554-graduarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to dismiss, then the Spanish for to resign.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: graduarse}
\textbf{graduarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to graduate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Se graduó en Medicina en 2020.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She graduated in Medicine in 2020.}
\end{quote}

It takes an accent: \emph{me gradúo}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{graduarse} is usually traced to Medieval Latin \emph{graduāre} 'to give a degree', built on Latin \emph{gradus} 'a step' (Lewis \& Short), the word behind \emph{grado}. To graduate is to take the next step.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{graduarse}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{graduarse}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{graduarse}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to dismiss, then the Spanish for to resign, then say \emph{graduarse} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does graduarse mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To graduate\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la graduación]{la graduación — the graduation}

\label{lesson:ES-C554-graduacion}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to resign, then the Spanish for to graduate.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la graduación}
\textbf{la graduación} — \textquotedblleft{}the graduation\textquotedblright{}.

Mis padres vinieron a mi graduación.

\emph{graduación} is built on \emph{graduar}, which is usually traced to Medieval Latin \emph{graduāre}, from Latin \emph{gradus} 'a step' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[licenciarse]{licenciarse — to get a degree, to graduate}

\label{lesson:ES-C554-licenciarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to graduate, then the Spanish for the graduation.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: licenciarse}
\textbf{licenciarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to get a degree, to graduate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Me licencié en Historia.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I got my degree in History.}
\end{quote}

Mostly in Spain: \emph{la licenciatura} is the degree.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{licenciarse} is built on \emph{licencia}, from Latin \emph{licentia} 'freedom, leave to act' (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{licet} 'it is allowed'. A degree was the licence to teach.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{licenciarse}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{licenciarse}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to graduate, then the Spanish for the graduation, then say \emph{licenciarse} again
\end{itemize}

\section[la mayoría de edad]{la mayoría de edad — the age of majority, adulthood}

\label{lesson:ES-C554-mayoria-de-edad}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the graduation, then the Spanish for to get a degree.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la mayoría de edad}
\textbf{la mayoría de edad} — \textquotedblleft{}the age of majority, adulthood\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Al cumplir la mayoría de edad, sacó el carné.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{When she came of age, she got her licence.}
\end{quote}

In Spain it is eighteen: \emph{ser mayor de edad} — to be an adult.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{la mayoría de edad} is built on \emph{mayoría}, from \emph{mayor}, which comes from Latin \emph{maior} 'greater', and \emph{edad}, from Latin \emph{aetās}, \emph{aetātem} 'age, lifetime' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la mayoría de edad}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la mayoría de edad}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the graduation, then the Spanish for to get a degree, then say \emph{la mayoría de edad} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[envejecer]{envejecer — to grow old, to age}

\label{lesson:ES-C554-envejecer}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to get a degree, then the Spanish for the age of majority.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: envejecer}
\textbf{envejecer} — \textquotedblleft{}to grow old, to age\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mi perro ha envejecido mucho.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My dog has aged a lot.}
\end{quote}

It takes a \emph{z}: \emph{envejezco}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{envejecer} is built on \emph{viejo} 'old' with \emph{en-} and \emph{-ecer}. \emph{Viejo} is inherited from Latin \emph{vetulus} 'little old', from \emph{vetus} 'old' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to get a degree, then the Spanish for the age of majority, then say \emph{envejecer} again
\end{itemize}
